title: Split EX into single-cycle integer ALU plus iterative DIV/REM unit
motivation:
All three baseline P&R seeds have the same critical path: ID/EX register ->
forward mux -> monolithic combinational ALU -> EX/MEM register (7.87 ns,
median 127.03 MHz). That ALU contains three soft 64-bit products plus fully
combinational signed/unsigned DIV and REM. The design uses 3704 Gowin ALU
carry cells and 9563 LUT4 for a 5-stage scalar core.

Measured evidence gathered for this hypothesis:
- Probe: identical bench RTL with only the DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU arms stubbed
  to 0, same synth.tcl + core_bench_si.sv + 3 nextpnr seeds. Fmax went
  148.32 / 150.58 / 139.10 MHz, median 148.3 vs 127.03 (+16.8%). LUT4 went
  9563 -> 4690 and ALU cells 3704 -> 308. The remaining critical path
  (6.74 ns) is ID/EX -> fwd mux -> ALU shift/logic mux -> final EX/MEM
  alu_result mux.
- A Verilator retirement trace of coremark.elf shows 2,922,016
  instructions between the start/stop markers, with ZERO
  DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU (93,960 MULs). Only 2 divides run in the whole program:
  1 before the bracket and 1 after it.
- Reference core v1 (read-only) made the same move from the same baseline
  ("Cold Multi-Cycle DIV/REM Unit"): Fmax 138 -> 160 MHz, LUT4
  10.2K -> 5.9K, fitness +16%, CoreMark cycles essentially unchanged.
  It was v1's largest single-step gain.

Why not other structural angles: a cycle-exact Python model of this
pipeline reproduced the measured stalled and unstalled cycle counts
exactly (3,483,582 / 4,302,170 / 3,675,518 / 4,491,485). With a decoupled
2-8 entry fetch queue plus empty-bypass, it only gets 4.49M -> 4.33M
cycles (-3.6%). Fetch bandwidth (0.78 words/cycle under the 22% imem
stall) is the ceiling. v1's elastic fetch skid buffer also regressed on
Fmax. Taking the divider off the universal EX path is the structural
change with by far the best measured payoff.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU out of the single-cycle ALU into a dedicated
multi-cycle divide unit that sits beside the ALU in EX, behind a
start/busy/done interlock. All RV32I ops, branches, loads/stores, jumps and
all four MUL variants stay single-cycle and bit-identical. Do NOT reshape
or re-time the multiplier: two v1 attempts dropped Fmax to 95-100 MHz.

1. div_unit (new): radix-2 restoring divider with one 33-bit
   subtract/compare plus shift per cycle. It takes absolute-value operands
   for signed ops and applies sign fixup at the end. Divide-by-zero and
   INT_MIN/-1 are resolved at start with no iteration, returning
   0xFFFFFFFF/dividend or INT_MIN/0 exactly as today. Result and done are
   registered outputs.
   Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS, keep the same start/busy/done handshake but
   use a fixed short latency (1-2 busy cycles) returning the existing ALTOPS
   formulas (moved here from alu.sv). This keeps insn/liveness within the
   depth-20 formal budget while still proving the stall/ordering logic.
2. EX (ex_stage) behavior while a divide is in EX:
   - On its first EX cycle, latch the post-forward rs1/rs2 values and start
     the unit. These latched values also feed RVFI rs1_rdata/rs2_rdata,
     because forwarding sources drain while the divide waits.
   - While busy, on every non-dmem-stall cycle, EX/MEM captures a bubble
     (valid=0, reg_write=0, no mem op). This makes older instructions
     retire exactly once.
   - On done, which stays sticky until EX/MEM can accept (!dmem_stall),
     EX/MEM captures the divide's full metadata and result.
   - Result injection must not add a LUT level to the critical
     ALU -> EX/MEM path. Merge it with the existing JAL/JALR link-value
     mux: alu_result_q <= use_alt ? alt_val : alu_result, where
     use_alt = is_jump | div_done and alt_val = div_done ? div_q : pc+4.
     Both selects and alt_val come only from registers, so the final mux
     stays 2:1 as today.
3. hazard_unit: new ex_div_busy input. While it is high, hold the PC and
   ID/EX (stall, not flush). Keep dmem_stall priority unchanged. A divide
   never redirects and is never a load, so load-use and redirect logic are
   untouched.
4. decoder/core_pkg: add a ctrl bit is_div. Set it only inside the
   already-validated funct7=0000001 arm when funct3[2]=1, so EX tests one
   registered bit instead of decoding alu_op. is_illegal defaults remain
   untouched.

Expected result: CoreMark bracketed cycles stay about 4.49M. Any change
should only be LFSR stall-phase noise from the one pre-bracket DIV now
taking ~34 cycles. A larger change means an interlock bug. Median Fmax
should rise to about 142-148 MHz, a bit under the 148.3 probe because of
the small divider and control added back. That gives fitness of roughly
282.82 -> ~320-330 iter/s.

title: Fetch-stage predecode + 64-entry bimodal BHT (zero-bubble correctly-predicted branches/JAL)
motivation:
The core has no branch prediction: next_pc is always pc+4, and every taken
BRANCH/JAL/JALR redirects from EX. IF and ID share one cycle (imem is read
combinationally from the PC register and there is no IF/ID flop), so each taken
control transfer costs exactly 1 bubble.

I measured this on the real fitness workload. The existing cosim_sim
(--istall --dstall, default seed) reproduces the logged 4,491,485 cycles. I
counted the RVFI stream between the 0x10000100 and 0x10000104 markers:
  - 2,922,015 instructions retired; CPI 1.537.
  - Branches are 18.1% of instructions. 294,425 of them are taken (10.1%).
    Backward branches are taken 82% of the time.
  - JAL: 49,367 (1.7%). JALR: 13,735 (0.47%), all of them returns.
  - Taken control transfers total 357,527, i.e. 357k bubble cycles, about 8.0%
    of all cycles. This is the second-largest overhead after bus stalls.
    Load-use accounts for 204k.
I replayed that trace through several predictors (cost = number of mispredicted
control transfers, 1 cycle each):
  - No prediction (today): 357.5k.
  - Static backward-taken/forward-not-taken: 125k.
  - Bimodal 2-bit, 32 entries: 69k. 64 entries: 65k. 256 entries: 58k.
    JAL is always predicted taken in all of these; JALR is not predicted.
  - Adding a 4-entry return stack saves only about 14k more (0.3%). Not worth
    a 32-bit compare on the forwarded JALR path.
  - gshare only beats bimodal at 1024 entries or more (38k). Too big for a
    design sitting at 9563 LUT4 against a 10k target.
So a small bimodal table plus fetch-time target computation captures about 82%
of the available control-flow gain. It needs no target storage and no tags.
Each correctly predicted taken branch saves exactly 1 cycle, even with random
imem stalls. The target fetch simply moves one cycle earlier, and the stall
probability on that fetch is unchanged.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Predict at fetch using the instruction that the fetch cycle already has
combinationally (imem_data). Verify in EX. Keep the 1-cycle mispredict penalty.

1. IF-stage predecode (if_stage.sv)
   - From the raw imem_data, detect BRANCH (opcode 1100011) and JAL
     (opcode 1101111).
   - Select the B-immediate or the J-immediate.
   - Compute pred_target = pc + imm. A 30-bit add on [31:2] is enough because
     pc[1:0] = 0 and imm[0] = 0.
   - Never predict when imm[1] = 1, i.e. instr[8] for B-type or instr[21] for
     J-type. That target would be misaligned, and EX's existing misalign trap
     must see a non-taken prediction.
   - Never predict JALR.
2. BHT (inside if_stage.sv)
   - 64 x 2-bit saturating counters. Use a flop array with synchronous reset
     to 2'b01. That keeps it deterministic for formal and cosim and avoids
     depending on SSRAM/LUT-RAM support in nextpnr-himbaechel.
   - Index with pc[7:2]. Read combinationally at fetch.
   - pred_taken_raw = is_jal_pd | (is_br_pd & bht[pc[7:2]][1]), and suppressed
     when imm[1] = 1.
   - One write port driven from EX.
3. next_pc
   - PC priority stays: redirect > stall > advance.
   - Advance = pred_taken_raw ? pred_target : pc+4. Keep the mux ordering as
     redirect ? redirect_target : (pred ? pred_target : pc+4), so the late
     EX-redirect signal still drives only the outermost mux level.
   - The prediction is naturally ignored whenever stall_if holds the PC
     (load-use, imem stall, dmem stall). The same PC is re-predicted from the
     refetched word next cycle. This matters for formal, where imem_data is a
     free value every cycle.
4. New pipeline fields (IF/ID bundle -> ID/EX register)
   - pred_taken: MUST be gated with the bundle's valid, i.e.
     pred_taken_raw & !(flush || redirect). A bubble captured during an imem
     stall or a flush must carry pred_taken = 0; otherwise EX would fire a
     spurious redirect.
   - bht_ctr[1:0]: the counter value read at fetch, used for the update.
   - alt_target = pred_taken ? pc+4 : pc+imm. This is the "other" path EX
     redirects to if it disagrees.
   - The ID/EX flush/reset path already zeroes the whole struct. That is
     required for all three fields.
5. EX (ex_stage.sv)
   - actual = (branch_taken | is_jump) & !misalign_fault. This is exactly
     today's redirect expression.
   - redirect = actual ^ in.pred_taken. This is now a mispredict signal. The
     hazard unit and if_stage keep consuming `redirect` unchanged, so
     flush_if/flush_id behave exactly as today: only on a mispredict.
   - redirect_target = in.ctrl.is_jalr ? {jalr_sum[31:1],1'b0} : in.alt_target.
     JALR is never predicted. A predicted-taken instruction that disagrees
     always goes to pc+4, and a non-predicted branch/JAL goes to pc+imm, both
     taken from alt_target. This takes the EX pc+imm adder off the
     redirect->PC path, which offsets the extra XOR level.
   - pc_next / RVFI pc_wdata logic is unchanged.
   - BHT update: when in.valid & in.ctrl.is_branch, write
     bht[in.pc[7:2]] <= branch_cond ? sat_inc(in.bht_ctr) : sat_dec(in.bht_ctr).
     Repeated writes while EX is held by a dmem stall are idempotent.
6. core.sv: wire the BHT write port (we, index, data) from ex_stage to
   if_stage.

Correctness argument
- pred_target is derived from the same instruction bits that are captured into
  ID/EX in that cycle. So a predicted-taken BRANCH/JAL always has the correct
  target; the only possible wrong outcome is direction. Counters may hold any
  value without affecting architectural state.
- Exactly one wrong-path instruction can exist (the one in fetch), and the
  existing flush_if/flush_id machinery kills it, as it does today.
- rvfi_order, pc_fwd/pc_bwd, unique, liveness and ill are unaffected. Trap
  discipline is unchanged: a misaligned target is never predicted, and a
  predicted instruction that faults redirects to pc+4.

Expected effect
- Cycles: about 4.49M -> 4.20M (-6.5%), i.e. +7.0% iterations/cycle.
- Fmax: the added fetch path is imem_data (an LFSR flop in the FPGA bench) ->
  1-level predecode/imm mux -> 30-bit carry chain -> 2-level PC mux, plus a
  parallel pc -> 64:1 counter mux. Both should sit well under the current
  7.87 ns ALU-limited critical path. The EX redirect path gains an XOR but
  loses the pc+imm adder on redirect_target.
- Area: about +150-200 LUT4 and about +165 FF (128 BHT flops + 33 new ID/EX
  bits). That stays under the 10k LUT target.

changes.description: Add pred_taken (1b), bht_ctr (2b), and alt_target (32b: pc+4 if predicted taken, else pc+imm) to if_id_t and id_ex_t.

Add BRANCH/JAL predecode from raw imem_data (B/J imm select, pc+imm target, suppress if imm[1]=1). Add a 64x2b bimodal BHT flop array (reset 2'b01) indexed by pc[7:2], with an EX-driven write port. next_pc = redirect ? redirect_target : (pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4). Emit pred_taken gated by !(flush||redirect), plus bht_ctr and alt_target, in the IF/ID bundle.
Pass pred_taken, bht_ctr and alt_target from the IF/ID bundle into the ID/EX register. The existing flush/reset-to-'0 keeps them zeroed on bubbles.
